title: Unconstitutional Comelec restrictions
primary_topics: CJ's constitutional challenge to Comelec's 'aggregate total' TV ad limit of 120 minutes as an unconstitutional prior restraint
The rule's perverse effect: disadvantaging new/poor/unknown candidates while favoring celebrities, incumbents, and dynasties
Free expression as a preferred constitutional right requiring strict scrutiny for content-based government restrictions

372 national/regional TV stations + 1,113 cable TV providers (NTC, June 2012)

stances.claim: The Comelec's 120-minute aggregate total TV ad limit is unconstitutional as a content-based prior restraint on free speech: under Chavez vs Gonzales, it must pass the 'clear and present danger' test — a burden the Comelec cannot meet — and CJ's own ABS-CBN vs Comelec requires courts to 'lean in favor of freedom' when campaign speech is restricted.
stances.rhetorical_move: strict-scrutiny application: using the preferred-right status of free expression to impose the highest constitutional burden on Comelec's restriction

stances.claim: The rule is perversely counterproductive to its stated goal of limiting rich-candidate propaganda: it most disadvantages new, poor, and unknown candidates who need TV exposure most, while celebrities, media hotshots, incumbents, and dynastic candidates with built-in name recall are the least affected.
stances.rhetorical_move: adverse-effect inversion: showing the rule achieves the opposite of its intended leveling purpose

stances.claim: TV is the most cost-efficient and pervasive campaign medium: at 4 centavos per viewer on Kapuso Mo Jessica Soho, it is cheaper than town rallies, helicopter hops, and distribution of election materials — making the restriction especially harmful to candidates with limited budgets.
stances.rhetorical_move: cost-efficiency data argument: Nielsen and NTC statistics as concrete proof of TV's democratic value for less-resourced candidates

notable_anecdotes: CJ's own ABS-CBN vs Comelec (January 28, 2000) — cited as ponente — establishing the 'lean in favor of freedom' doctrine for campaign speech cases, making this column a self-referential application of his own landmark ruling to the 2013 Comelec restriction.

The Nielsen Philippines calculation: a 30-second ad on 'Kapuso Mo Jessica Soho' reaches 9,509,573 viewers at P419,265, or 4 centavos per person — CJ's deployment of advertiser data to make the constitutional argument about TV's democratic efficiency viscerally concrete.

The arithmetic devastation: 120 aggregate minutes ÷ 87 campaign days = 82.75 seconds per day for all networks; divided by 3 major networks = 27.58 seconds each — 'barely enough for only one—yes, one—TV spot of 30 seconds' per day per network.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that the Comelec's resolution imposing an 'aggregate total' of only 120 TV minutes and 180 radio minutes per national candidate for the entire 87-day campaign period is 'unconstitutional, unfair and unwise.' The arithmetic is stark: 120 aggregate minutes divided by 87 days equals 82.75 seconds per day across all networks -- with only three major networks, each candidate gets 27.58 seconds per network per day, 'barely enough for only one--yes, one--TV spot of 30 seconds.' He grounds the constitutional argument in Chavez vs Gonzales (free expression is a preferred right subject to clear-and-present-danger scrutiny for content-based restrictions), Justice Carpio's concurrence (no prior restraint), and his own ABS-CBN vs Comelec ponencia (courts must 'lean in favor of freedom' when campaign speech is restricted). He demonstrates the rule's perverse effect using Nielsen data: a 30-second spot on Kapuso Mo Jessica Soho reaches 9,509,573 viewers at only 4 centavos per person -- making TV the most cost-efficient medium for new, poor, and unknown candidates who most need exposure. The rule instead benefits celebrities, media hotshots, incumbents, and dynastic candidates with built-in name recall, directly contradicting its stated goal of limiting wealthy-candidate propaganda. He proposes campaign expense limits as a constitutionally permissible alternative that levels the field without suppressing speech.
